issues.legal_issue: A final decree and an auction sale founded on a preliminary mortgage decree do not remain effective when an appellate preliminary decree substitutes that decree and the mortgagor fulfils the substituted terms.
material_facts: A trial court passed a preliminary mortgage decree that allowed payment by instalments and permitted a final decree for sale if the mortgagors defaulted.
While an appeal from that preliminary decree was pending, the trial court passed a final decree for sale and the property was sold in execution of it.
The parties later agreed to, and the appellate court passed, a substituted preliminary decree that fixed the amount payable; the mortgagor paid the amount and the decree was recorded as satisfied.
The judgment debtor challenged the execution and sale under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: The substituted appellate preliminary decree displaced the original preliminary decree. Because the mortgagor fulfilled the substituted decree, there was no basis to maintain the application for sale; the auction sale and its confirmation became non-est, and the judgment debtor’s objection was sustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(2) and its Explanation to the Code of Civil Procedure, a preliminary decree requires further proceedings before the suit is completely disposed of, while a final decree completely disposes of it. In a mortgage suit governed by Order 34, the final decree for sale must accord with the operative preliminary decree. An appellate decree may redefine the parties’ obligations, and rights arising from the displaced decree cannot be retained while those obligations are replaced. Questions concerning execution, discharge or satisfaction are determined under Section 47 by the executing court. The Court distinguished the protection of a stranger auction purchaser discussed in Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh, [1967] 2 SCR 77, and considered Hukumchand v. Bansilal, [1967] 3 SCR 695, and Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai, [1982] 2 SCR 186.

rule.if: mortgage_suit_execution_objection and appellate_preliminary_decree_substituted and sale_executed_under_old_final_decree and mortgagor_fulfilled_substituted_terms

predicates.mortgage_suit_execution_objection: A judgment debtor raises an objection in execution of a decree arising from a mortgage suit.
predicates.appellate_preliminary_decree_substituted: An appellate court replaces the preliminary decree with a substituted preliminary decree.
predicates.sale_executed_under_old_final_decree: The property is sold under a final decree founded on the preliminary decree that was replaced.
predicates.mortgagor_fulfilled_substituted_terms: The mortgagor fulfils the payment obligations imposed by the substituted preliminary decree.
predicates.auction_sale_is_non_est: The auction sale and its confirmation have no continuing legal effect.

issues.definition: When a judgment debtor objects in execution of a mortgage suit decree, an appellate substituted preliminary decree replaces the basis of an old final decree sale, and the mortgagor fulfils the substituted terms, the sale has no continuing legal effect.

issues.legal_issue: An auction purchaser under a final mortgage decree is not deemed a party to the suit at the preliminary-decree stage merely by purchasing at the later sale.
material_facts: The auction purchasers acquired the property at a sale held in execution of a final decree for sale.
The sale occurred after the trial court had passed its preliminary decree.
The appellate court later substituted the preliminary decree by consent of the suit parties, without the auction purchasers participating in that settlement.
The judgment debtor relied on Section 47 to challenge the sale after the substituted decree was satisfied.
issues.conclusion: The auction purchasers could not claim to be parties to the suit at or before the preliminary-decree stage on the basis of their later purchase, so their participation was not required for the substituted preliminary decree.
issues.legal_principle: Explanation II(a) to Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure deems a purchaser at a sale in execution of a decree to be a party to the suit in which that decree was passed. In a suit under Order 34, the preliminary and final decrees are stages in the same suit, but the property is not sold in execution of the preliminary decree. A purchaser at the later sale cannot therefore be treated as a party at the earlier preliminary-decree stage. Questions relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction are determined under Section 47.

predicates.mortgage_suit_with_preliminary_and_final: A mortgage suit proceeds through a preliminary decree and a later final decree.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_property_under_final_: A purchaser acquires the property at a sale held in execution of the final decree.
predicates.purchase_occurred_after_preliminary_decr: The purchaser acquires the property only after the preliminary decree has been passed.
predicates.purchaser_not_deemed_party_at_preliminar: The purchaser is not treated as a party to the suit at the preliminary-decree stage.

issues.definition: When a purchaser acquires property only at a sale under a final decree in a mortgage suit, the purchaser is not treated as a party at the earlier preliminary-decree stage.

issues.legal_issue: A court may direct compensation for auction purchasers whose purchase money remains blocked when a sale is set aside because a substituted preliminary decree removes the basis for the sale.
material_facts: The auction purchasers’ purchase money had remained deposited in court since the sale proceedings began.
The substituted preliminary decree was satisfied, removing the basis for the final decree sale and its confirmation.
The Court held that the strict compensation provision in Order 34, Rule 5(2) did not apply because that stage had not arrived in law.
The judgment debtor’s appeal was allowed subject to a direction to pay the auction purchasers interest on their blocked purchase money.
issues.conclusion: Although compensation was not due under the strict terms of Order 34, Rule 5(2), the Court directed payment to the auction purchasers of a sum equivalent to the blocked purchase money, exercising its inherent powers under the Code and its powers under Article 142 to do complete justice.
issues.legal_principle: Order 34, Rule 5(2) provides for a compensatory deposit in the circumstances specified by that rule, but those circumstances had not arisen here because the relevant stage had been rendered non-est. The Court nevertheless exercised its inherent powers under the Code of Civil Procedure and its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to further the cause of complete justice and to be fair to the auction purchasers.

rule.if: appeal_by_judgment_debtor and mortgage_sale_set_aside_after_substituted_decree_satisfied and purchaser_money_remained_blocked and statutory_compensation_stage_not_reached

predicates.appeal_by_judgment_debtor: A judgment debtor appeals after an objection to execution and sale has been rejected.
predicates.mortgage_sale_set_aside_after_substitute: A mortgage sale is set aside after the mortgagor satisfies a substituted preliminary decree.
predicates.purchaser_money_remained_blocked: The auction purchasers’ money remains deposited and unavailable to them.
predicates.statutory_compensation_stage_not_reached: The procedural stage that would entitle the purchasers to compensation under the applicable mortgage-sale rule has not been reached.
predicates.court_directs_compensation_for_auction_p: The court directs that compensation be paid to the auction purchasers.

issues.definition: When a judgment debtor’s appeal results in a mortgage sale being set aside after satisfaction of a substituted decree, and the purchasers’ money remains blocked without the statutory compensation stage having been reached, the court directs compensation for the purchasers.
